transcript.text: Salieri. I have received letters — more than one — alleging that you have used your position as Kapellmeister to suppress the works of rival composers and to block appointments to the Court that do not serve your personal interests. These are serious charges for a man in your position. I value your service, but I must hear your account. Explain yourself.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
Your Majesty, I am deeply honored by this audience and grateful for the opportunity to address these troubling accusations. Allow me to clarify the situation regarding the appointments to the Court and the scheduling of operas.

As Kapellmeister, it is my duty to ensure that the musical standards of the Court are upheld and that only the most deserving composers are granted prestigious positions. I assure Your Majesty that my decisions are based solely on the merit of the composers and their works, not on personal interests or rivalries.

Regarding the scheduling of operas, it is true that I have been involved in the selection process. As a composer myself, I have a keen ear for quality music and a responsibility to uphold the reputation of the Court's musical performances. If any decisions I have made have been perceived as unfair, I apologize and am willing to reconsider them.

I assure Your Majesty that my only intention is to serve the Court with the utmost dedication and respect for the art of music. If there are any specific instances you would like me to address or further explain, I am at your disposal.

transcript.text: Merit, you say. Very well. Let us speak of merit. There is talk of a certain composer—Mozart, I believe—whose works have been passed over for performance here at Court, despite their popularity in Vienna. His *Figaro* was a sensation, yet I do not recall it gracing our stage. Was that a judgment of its merit? Or perhaps something else?

Your Majesty, I am aware of the talented composer Mozart and his opera *Figaro*, which indeed garnered much acclaim in Vienna. It is true that *Figaro* has not been performed on our Court stage, and I understand your concern regarding this matter.

As Kapellmeister, it is my responsibility to curate the opera season and select works that align with the Court's artistic vision and standards. While I recognize the merit and popularity of Mozart's compositions, decisions regarding the inclusion of specific works in the season lineup are based on various factors, including the overall balance of the program, the availability of resources, and the artistic direction of the Court's musical offerings.

In the case of *Figaro*, the decision not to include it in the season was not a reflection of its lack of merit, but rather a result of the considerations mentioned earlier. I hold Mozart's talent in high regard, and I have no personal animosity towards him or his works. My aim has always been to uphold the musical excellence of our Court while also considering the diverse range of repertoire available to us.

If *Figaro* has not been given the opportunity to be performed at Court, I am willing to revisit the programming decisions and explore the possibility of including it in future seasons. Your Majesty's desire to showcase outstanding works of music is commendable, and I am committed to working towards fulfilling that goal while maintaining the standards that define our Court's musical legacy.

transcript.text: You speak of balance, of resources, of artistic direction. These are the words of an administrator. I appointed you not merely as an administrator, but as a judge of musical genius. Tell me plainly: do you believe Mozart's *Figaro* to be a work of genius? And if you do, how can such a work be excluded for the sake of 'balance'? The people of Vienna flocked to it. transcript.speaker: roleplayer

Your Majesty, I stand by my previous statement that Mozart's *Figaro* is indeed a work of genius. As Kapellmeister, I am entrusted with the responsibility of making difficult decisions regarding our Court's musical programming. The exclusion of *Figaro* from our stage was not a reflection of its merit or lack thereof, but rather a result of the careful balancing act required to maintain a dynamic and engaging repertoire.

Your Majesty, I understand the importance of recognizing and celebrating true genius in music. If there has been any oversight in the programming of Mozart's works, I am willing to reevaluate our approach and ensure that his masterpieces receive the attention and acclaim they deserve at Court. I am committed to upholding the standards of excellence that you have entrusted me with, and I will strive to honor the genius of composers like Mozart in our Court's musical endeavors.

transcript.text: A careful balancing act. You admit the work is genius, yet you excluded it. This begins to sound less like administration and more like... caution. Or perhaps fear. Are you afraid, Salieri? Afraid that such a flame might outshine your own compositions? I have always valued your work, but I value truth more. Did you keep *Figaro* from my stage to protect your own standing?

transcript.text:
Your Majesty, I understand your concerns and I must address them with utmost honesty and humility. It is true that I have felt a certain sense of caution in my decisions regarding the Court's repertoire, including the exclusion of Mozart's "The Marriage of Figaro." While I have always strived to uphold the standards of excellence in my role as Kapellmeister, I cannot deny that there may have been moments of self-doubt and apprehension.

I must confess that the shadow of Mozart's immense talent and burgeoning reputation has cast a long shadow over my own work. His compositions have garnered widespread acclaim and adoration, while my own have perhaps not received the same level of recognition. In moments of weakness, I may have succumbed to feelings of insecurity and fear that Mozart's brilliance would indeed outshine my own modest contributions.

Your Majesty, I deeply regret any actions that may have been driven by such emotions. It was never my intention to stifle the creativity of a fellow composer out of personal concerns. I have always strived to serve the Court to the best of my abilities, and I see now that true artistic integrity requires me to rise above such petty rivalries and embrace the genius of others.

I humbly ask for your forgiveness and understanding as I confront my own shortcomings and commit to a future of greater openness, generosity, and respect for the talents of all composers, including the incomparable Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. Your guidance and wisdom are invaluable to me, and I pledge to honor them in my future endeavors as Kapellmeister.

transcript.text: This is a more honest answer. I appreciate your candor, though it troubles me. A Kapellmeister who fears a rival's genius is like a general who fears a better sword.
